payload.title: Required community service
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original sources — summaries of three (fictional) peer-reviewed studies.

Source 1: A survey of alumni
Researchers surveyed 800 adults who graduated from high school five years earlier. Of the 400 who had completed required service hours in high school, 46 percent reported volunteering in the past year. Of the 400 who had not been required to complete service, 31 percent reported volunteering. The researchers pointed out that students were not assigned to the two kinds of schools and that other differences between the schools may account for the results.

Source 2: A field experiment
Researchers randomly assigned 120 students at one school to a Required group (60 students), who had to complete 20 service hours, or an Optional group (60 students), who were invited to complete service hours if they wished. Six months later, the researchers recorded the number of hours that students chose to volunteer when no hours were required. The Required group's mean was 4 hours and the Optional group's mean was 9 hours. The difference was statistically significant.

Source 3: Interviews with students
Researchers interviewed 40 students about their service experiences. Of the 40, 28 said that after helping at a local shelter they felt more confident that they could make a difference in their community. Fifteen of those who completed required hours described the hours as 'something I had to get done.' The researchers noted that students who agreed to be interviewed may have had stronger opinions than others.

payload.title: Spaced learning
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original sources — summaries of three (fictional) peer-reviewed studies.

Source 1: A laboratory experiment
Researchers randomly assigned 100 adults to learn 60 unfamiliar foreign words in one of two ways. The Massed group (50 adults) studied the words in one 60-minute session. The Spaced group (50 adults) studied for 20 minutes on each of three days. All participants were tested on the words one week later. The mean number of words recalled was 21 in the Massed group and 33 in the Spaced group. The difference was statistically significant.

Source 2: A classroom study of weekly quizzes
In one school district, 12 history classes were randomly selected to give a short cumulative quiz each week (Quiz classes), and 12 classes used no weekly quizzes (No-quiz classes). The same teacher taught one Quiz class and one No-quiz class, and all classes took the same final exam. The mean final exam score was 84 percent in the Quiz classes and 78 percent in the No-quiz classes. The researchers reported that the difference was statistically significant.

Source 3: A survey of study habits
Researchers surveyed 500 high school students. Of the students, 70 percent said that studying a lot the night before a test works better than studying a little each day. When the researchers compared the students' reported study methods with their exam grades, they found that students who reported studying a little each day earned higher grades on average than students who reported cramming. Students who volunteered for the survey were more likely to be in advanced classes.

payload.title: Team bonuses
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original sources — summaries of three (fictional) peer-reviewed studies.

Source 1: A laboratory experiment on effort
Researchers asked 80 students to pull on a rope-pulling machine that measured force. In the Alone condition (40 students), each student believed that his or her own force was measured. In the Team condition (40 students), each student believed that only the total force of a four-person team was measured. Students in the Alone condition produced a mean force of 100 units, and students in the Team condition produced a mean force of 78 units. The difference was statistically significant.

Source 2: A survey of employee burnout
Researchers surveyed 500 employees at a large company about their workload and their sense of burnout. Employees who said that the amount of work in their team was shared unfairly reported more burnout, and the correlation between perceived unfairness of workload and burnout was r = +0.44. Employees who volunteered to answer the survey were more likely to work in teams that rewarded group results.

Source 3: A field study of two sales offices
Researchers compared two sales offices of the same company for one year. Office A paid a bonus based on each salesperson's own sales (individual bonus), and Office B paid a bonus based on the sales of the entire office (team bonus). Office A's mean monthly sales per person were $52,000 and Office B's were $47,000. Employees were not randomly assigned to the offices, and Office B was in a region with lower average incomes.

stimulus.description: Summary of the key results in the three sources

rows: Mean force: 100 units (Alone) vs 78 units (Team); statistically significant
r = +0.44 between perceived unfair workload and burnout
Mean monthly sales per person: $52,000 (individual bonus) vs $47,000 (team bonus); employees not randomly assigned

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim, based in psychological science, that responds to the question: Should a company reward employees mainly with team-based bonuses instead of individual bonuses?
parts.model_answer: ALTON reference answer for self-review — not official AP scoring. A company should not rely mainly on team-based bonuses, because people put in less effort when their individual contribution cannot be identified.

rubric_rows.criterion: Proposes a specific and defensible claim that responds to the question
required_elements: Proposes a claim that is relevant to the question and takes a position or states a specific effect or recommendation (not a restatement of the question or an oversimplified conclusion)
alt_solutions: A company should combine individual and team rewards, because team bonuses alone reduce effort and unfair workloads are linked to burnout.
A company should reward individuals for their own contributions while encouraging teamwork.
common_errors: describes the question without making a claim
proposes a claim that is unrelated to the question
states that the issue is difficult or complicated without taking a position
rubric_rows.grading_note: Award the point when the response conveys the required meaning, whatever the wording; do not require any specific phrase.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Support your claim with one specific and relevant piece of evidence from one of the three sources. Cite the source (for example, 'Source 1').
parts.model_answer: ALTON reference answer for self-review — not official AP scoring. Source 1: students in the Team condition produced a mean force of 78 units, compared with 100 units for students in the Alone condition.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses one specific, accurate, and correctly cited piece of evidence from one source
required_elements: Cites one source (Source 1, 2, or 3) and gives specific and relevant evidence from it that supports the student's claim
alt_solutions: Source 1: 78 units versus 100 units of force
Source 2: r = +0.44 between unfair workload and burnout
Source 3: $52,000 versus $47,000 in monthly sales
common_errors: gives evidence with no citation
gives a vague statement such as 'people work less in groups'
gives evidence that is not relevant to the claim
rubric_rows.grading_note: Award the point when the response conveys the required meaning, whatever the wording; do not require any specific phrase.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence you used in part B supports your claim, using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding that you learned in AP Psychology.
parts.model_answer: ALTON reference answer for self-review — not official AP scoring. Social loafing: people tend to put in less effort when working in a group because their individual effort is not identifiable, which is why the Team condition produced less force.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains the relationship between the evidence and the claim
required_elements: explains how the evidence supports the claim: effort was lower when only team performance was measured, which supports not relying on team bonuses
links the difference in force to the claim
alt_solutions: people worked less in the team, so team bonuses are bad
a correct equivalent statement in the student's own words
common_errors: identifies the evidence without explaining how it relates to the claim
gives an opinion that does not refer to the sources
rubric_rows.grading_note: Award the point when the response conveys the required meaning, whatever the wording; do not require any specific phrase.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding
required_elements: Applies a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding from the course, such as social loafing, diffusion of responsibility, or social facilitation, to explain how the evidence supports the claim
alt_solutions: social loafing
diffusion of responsibility: each person feels less responsible in a team
individual effort was not identifiable in the team condition
common_errors: uses a concept that is only a term from the source such as 'sleep' or 'mean' or 'survey'
uses the same concept as in the earlier explanation part
rubric_rows.grading_note: Award the point when the response conveys the required meaning, whatever the wording; do not require any specific phrase.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Support your claim with an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the source you used in part B. Cite the source.
parts.model_answer: ALTON reference answer for self-review — not official AP scoring. Source 2: employees who said the workload in their team was shared unfairly reported more burnout, with a correlation of r = +0.44.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses one specific, accurate, and correctly cited piece of evidence from a different source than part B
required_elements: Cites a different source from the one used in part B and gives specific and relevant evidence from it that supports the claim
alt_solutions: Source 3: $52,000 versus $47,000
Source 2: r = +0.44 between unfair workload and burnout
Source 1: 78 versus 100 units (if Source 2 or 3 was used in part B)
common_errors: uses the same source as part B
gives evidence with no citation
gives evidence that is not relevant to the claim
rubric_rows.grading_note: Award the point when the response conveys the required meaning, whatever the wording; do not require any specific phrase.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence you used in part D supports your claim, using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding than the one you used in part C.
parts.model_answer: ALTON reference answer for self-review — not official AP scoring. Burnout is a work-related stress response (distress) that can build when team rewards leave some members carrying more of the load; fairer, individually tracked rewards reduce that source of stress, which supports not relying mainly on team bonuses.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains the relationship between the evidence and the claim
required_elements: explains how the evidence supports the claim: sales were higher in the office that tied the reward to individual results
links the sales difference to the claim
alt_solutions: the individual bonus office sold more, so individual bonuses are better
a correct equivalent statement in the student's own words
common_errors: identifies the evidence without explaining how it relates to the claim
gives an opinion that does not refer to the sources
rubric_rows.grading_note: Award the point when the response conveys the required meaning, whatever the wording; do not require any specific phrase.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding
required_elements: Applies a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding from the course than the one used in part C, such as incentive theory, extrinsic motivation, positive reinforcement, burnout in industrial-organizational psychology, or distress, to explain how the evidence supports the claim
alt_solutions: incentive theory: rewards motivate behavior
extrinsic motivation from the individual bonus
burnout is a work-related stress response, so unfair workloads in teams can hurt employees
common_errors: uses a concept that is only a term from the source such as 'sleep' or 'mean' or 'survey'
uses the same concept as in the earlier explanation part
rubric_rows.grading_note: Award the point when the response conveys the required meaning, whatever the wording; do not require any specific phrase.

review.summary: The set-up and content are sound, but the E1 rubric row requires Source 3 sales evidence while the model answer and the D alternatives use Source 2. C1 is similarly locked to Source 1. Correct student responses would be scored inconsistently, so the scoring fails.

key_scoring.notes: Rubric rows C1 and E1 are tied to fixed sources (C1 to Source 1 effort, E1 to Source 3 sales). The E1 criterion requires 'sales were higher in the office with individual bonuses', but the model answer for D/E uses Source 2 (burnout) and the D alt solutions allow any different source. A student who correctly cites and explains Source 2 or Source 1 in D/E would be denied E1. The same problem affects C1 if a student cites Source 2 or 3 in B. Rows must be written source-agnostically, as in the official EBQ rubric, or the model answer must match.

difficulty.label: exam_prep
difficulty.rationale: AQ-style argumentation item (skill 4.B) requiring a defensible claim, two pieces of evidence from different sources, and two different psychological concepts (e.g., social loafing/diffusion of responsibility, correlation vs causation, sampling bias, confounds, experimental control). Concepts are in CED scope and the sources are short and explicit about their limitations. Multiple defensible claims are acceptable, so there is no unfair ambiguity. Difficulty comes from integrating evidence and concepts across five scored parts, which fits a full mock exam.
